titre: A Missing Link Made From an Ape's Jaw
accroche: For forty-one years, Piltdown passed for humanity's ancestor. An orangutan jaw and a human skull were all it took
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1912, Charles Dawson, an amateur antiquarian, announces that he has found near the village of Piltdown, in Sussex, fragments of a human-looking skull in Pleistocene gravels. With Arthur Smith Woodward, keeper of geology at the Natural History Museum, he presents the discovery to the Geological Society. They propose an age of 500,000 years. The “missing link” between ape and man seems to have been found, and in England.

The Natural History Museum describes a good-faith acceptance. The skull was human, the jaw apelike: exactly what one expected of a transitional being.

## What brought the object down

It was not a rival discovery that brought it down, but measurements. In 1949, Kenneth Oakley, a geologist at the Museum, applies the fluorine test to the bone: the remains would be only about 50,000 years old, which already ruled them out as a missing link, since *Homo sapiens* existed by then.

In 1953, Joseph Weiner, Kenneth Oakley, and Wilfrid Le Gros Clark demonstrate the rest. Skull and jaw come from two species, a human and, very probably, an orangutan. Under the microscope, the teeth bear scratches: they were filed down to give them human wear. Most of the pieces were stained to match the color of the gravels.

## What DNA added

In 2016, Isabelle De Groote and her colleagues take up the case again with tools that 1953 did not have. The mitochondrial DNA of the Piltdown I canine and the Piltdown II molar carries the same haplotype: a Bornean orangutan, probably from southwestern Sarawak. The jaw, the canine, and the molar very likely come from a single animal. The skull, for its part, comes from at least two humans, perhaps medieval. An old radiocarbon date for the jaw, with a margin of error of 90 to 120 years, is compatible with a Victorian or Edwardian collection specimen; the authors nonetheless urge taking it with great caution.

Above all, the pieces share a single modus operandi: brown staining, gravel packed into the cavities, putty rich in zinc and zirconium. The authors conclude that a single forger is at work, “most probably Charles Dawson.” The wording is cautious, and deliberately so: at least twenty other people have been accused over the years.

## The shift

The affair is not that of a perfect fake. The jaw was visibly an ape's, and the fraud held because it delivered the expected result, with authentic pieces from real species. The check that exposed it was simple and available: a microscope, a chemical test.

One question remains that the file does not settle: who else would have checked, if the fossil had contradicted expectations rather than flattering them?

repere.texte: The jaw, canine, and molar of Piltdown very probably come from a single Bornean orangutan. An old radiocarbon date, with a margin of error of 90 to 120 years, is compatible with a collection specimen, not with a 500,000-year-old fossil.
repere.source: De Groote et al., “New genetic and morphological evidence suggests a single hoaxer created “Piltdown man”,” Royal Society Open Science, 2016

carte.punch: The English “missing link”: an orangutan jaw with filed-down teeth.
carte.idee: In 1912, Piltdown passes for humanity's ancestor. In 1953, the microscope shows filed teeth and stained bones. In 2016, DNA identifies a Bornean orangutan and a single forger, most probably Dawson.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: De Groote et al. (2016) — New genetic and morphological evidence suggests a single hoaxer created “Piltdown man”
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: In English; the discussion of the suspects can be read without any background in paleoanthropology.

quiz.question: What made it possible to expose the Piltdown fraud in 1953?
choix: Microscopic examination of the teeth and the staining, which shows two species and alterations
The discovery of an older fossil, which contradicted Piltdown's chronology
Charles Dawson's confession, recorded before his death
A DNA test comparing the skull with that of orangutans
quiz.explication: In 1953, skull and jaw are recognized as belonging to two species, the teeth bear file scratches, and the bones are stained: these are physical and chemical examinations. No rival fossil or confession is involved, and DNA came only in 2016.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What animal species supplies the Piltdown jaw, according to the 2016 genetic study?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The mitochondrial DNA of the canine and molar matches a Bornean orangutan, probably from southwestern Sarawak.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why do the 2016 authors conclude there was a single forger?
choix: Because all the pieces share the same staining, the same packed gravel, and the same putty
Because Dawson left a written confession
Because the skull and the jaw come from the same individual
Because the digs lasted only one summer
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The modus operandi is consistent from piece to piece. That points to a single forger, “most probably” Dawson, without definitive proof.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the fluorine test of 1949, applied by Kenneth Oakley, show?
choix: That the remains were about 50,000 years old, so could not be a missing link
That the remains were 500,000 years old, as announced
That the jaw was recent and the skull ancient
That the remains came from Borneo
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Natural History Museum gives an age of about 50,000 years, which ruled out the missing link. The fraud itself was not established until 1953.
